summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints. Sexual-orientation grounds were written into constitutional protection in 1996, and the Civil Union Act of 2006 provides for same-sex marriage.

Criminalisation ended definitively in the 1990s. Sodomy and the common-law 'unnatural sexual offence' were struck down by the Constitutional Court in the National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality judgment of 1998, applied retroactively to 27 April 1994; the residual disparity that kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts was equalised at a gender-neutral 16 by the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act of 2007, and the Constitutional Court confirmed the old disparity unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, again retroactive to 1994. A visitor engages no consensual-conduct offence on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation.

The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed into law in May 2024, explicitly names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds, with hate speech requiring a 'clear intention' to be harmful, incite harm or promote hatred. Human Rights Watch and other legal commentators warned before enactment that the wording is vague and burdens free expression; the protection is nonetheless now a statutory offence framework rather than only a sentencing consideration, as it was before PEPUDA.

Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which allows amendment of sex status in the population registry and the issue of identity documents and passports reflecting gender identity. The statute requires medical or surgical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy; sex reassignment surgery is not required. Identity documents remain strictly binary, so non-binary people cannot be recognised, and the medical requirements are criticised as pathologising and as locking people out of recognition altogether. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards, with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, but officials confirmed the change would take a few years as it passes through consultation to legislation.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled for a transgender inmate, Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena, against the Department of Correctional Services in case 2024/070075. The court held that refusing to provide prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care in custody, and ordered the Department to provide gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, to implement required accommodations, and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities. Lawyers for Human Rights, which represented the inmate, had earlier in 2025 been litigating a transgender prisoner's conditions of detention while rights organisations questioned whether the Department's standard operating procedure was being implemented in practice; the judgment converts those obligations into binding equality-court remedies.

Mismatched documents remain a daily hazard. An analysis published in January 2026 by Mikhail Petersen of Gender Dynamix describes trans people facing humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for 'fraud' when presenting identity documents that do not match their presentation, and argues that legal gender recognition should be a right grounded in dignity. Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records a trans woman turned away from filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID, with police mocking her. Ordinary administrative tasks therefore carry an outing and refusal risk even though the underlying legal framework is protective.

Facilities access is contested rather than settled. A 2024 academic analysis in PER/PELJ, 'Did the CPA Shut the Bathroom Door?', examines whether gender-segregated bathrooms excluding transgender and non-binary people constitute unfair discrimination under the Promotion of Equality Act read with section 9 of the Constitution, and concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access. A trans visitor should expect facility rules to vary by venue and institution rather than to rest on a single settled national rule.

Gender-affirming care is lawful and available but unevenly distributed. Hormone therapy can be accessed from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Private care is concentrated in the major cities and public systems face long waits, which forces rural patients to travel to urban centres; in December 2024 LGBT activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long treatment delays for trans healthcare.

Violence against visibly trans people remains the principal physical risk. On 26 December 2024 the 23-year-old trans woman Aobakwe Mahlobo was attacked without provocation at a tavern in Tshwane, sustaining severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's December 2024 rights watch recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders in that month alone. Lesbians and trans people have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape', including among pupils, and activists have accused police of negligent handling of cases, including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, with impunity condemned by ActionAid. Protection machinery exists — a Department of Justice National Task Team from 2011, a National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities from April 2014 with a rapid response team for unsolved cases, a Justice Ministry programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence launched in the 2010s, and the 2024 Hate Crimes Act — but enforcement records remain uneven.

Partner and family recognition is broad: the Civil Union Act has been in force since 2006, and court decisions extending to same-sex couples cover immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits, and joint adoption.
